title: ENGR 510 B - Finite Element Analysis for Practicing Engineers

questions.q: What kind of course is Engineering 510 B?
options: A Brief continuing education course in Anderson Engineering: an overview and six lectures, about an hour
A software training course for one program
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.1: Paragraph 0.1 gives the format.
A is wrong: A Brief course is a first hour.
C is wrong: It is continuing education.
D is wrong: No particular software is assumed.

questions.q: What is the backbone of this course?
options: MIT OpenCourseWare 2.092/2.093, taught by Professor Klaus-Jürgen Bathe, with his Finite Element Procedures video course
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.8: The wording is original to the Academy.
A is wrong: That backs Probability and Statistics.
C is wrong: That backs Linear Algebra.
D is wrong: That backs Physics One.

questions.q: What habit runs through every lecture?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.11: Know roughly what the answer should be before trusting a result.
A is wrong: Not the habit named.
B is wrong: The course warns against that.
C is wrong: The opposite.

questions.q: Who named the finite element method, and when?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.2: Turner, Clough, Martin, and Topp published the stiffness method in 1956.
B is wrong: Courant used triangles for torsion earlier.
C is wrong: That is the MIT course date.
D is wrong: Irons introduced the patch test.

questions.q: What does the fact that each row of a spring stiffness matrix sums to zero mean?
options: Moving both nodes together produces no force
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.4: Symmetry reflects reciprocity.
A is wrong: It has stiffness k.
B is wrong: Unsupported, it is singular.
D is wrong: Only for rigid motion.

questions.q: What is the axial stiffness of a bar of length L, area A, and Young's modulus E?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.5: A steel bar with E = 200 GPa, A = 100 mm², L = 1 m has stiffness 20 kN/mm.
B is wrong: Stiffness grows with area, not length.
C is wrong: Area increases stiffness.
D is wrong: That has the wrong units for stiffness.

questions.q: When two springs share a node, what happens to their stiffness terms in the global matrix?
options: They add on that node's diagonal entry, giving k1 + k2
The larger one replaces the smaller
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.6: Each element adds its matrix at the positions of its own nodes; this is assembly.
A is wrong: Assembly adds element contributions.
C is wrong: Both contribute.
D is wrong: Only off-diagonal terms are negative.

questions.q: Why is the stiffness matrix of an unsupported structure singular?
options: Because the elements are too small
Because the loads are too large
Because rigid-body motions produce no force, so the displacements are not determined
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.8: A body in a plane has three rigid-body motions; in space it has six.
A is wrong: Element size does not cause singularity.
B is wrong: Load size does not matter.
C is wrong: Linear materials give perfectly solvable systems once supported.

questions.q: Two springs k1 and k2 in series are fixed at node one with force F at node three. What is the displacement of node three?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.9: Springs in series add their flexibilities.
B is wrong: That is for springs in parallel.
C is wrong: Displacement is force divided by stiffness.
D is wrong: Spring k1 also stretches.

questions.q: Which check should be made on every model after solution?
options: The stiffness matrix has no zero entries
The sum of the reactions balances the sum of the applied loads
The maximum stress is below one megapascal
The number of elements is even
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.10: If they do not balance, something is wrong with the loads or supports.
A is wrong: Most entries are zero in a sparse matrix.
C is wrong: That is not a general check.
D is wrong: Element count is irrelevant.

questions.q: In the steel bar example with 10 kN on 100 mm², what is the stress?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.11: Strain is five ten-thousandths; E times strain gives the same.
A is wrong: Off by a factor of ten.
B is wrong: Off by a factor of ten.
C is wrong: 0.5 mm is the stretch.

questions.q: A solver reports a singular matrix and huge displacements. What is the most likely cause?
options: A missing support or a disconnected part
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.15: Look for the rigid-body motion you forgot to prevent.
B is wrong: Not the usual cause.
C is wrong: Display does not affect solution.
D is wrong: Stiffness does not cause singularity.

questions.q: What is the weak form of the bar equation obtained by?
options: Multiplying by a test function, integrating over the length, and integrating by parts
Replacing E by a constant of one
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.3: The result must hold for every admissible test function.
A is wrong: It lowers, not raises, the derivatives.
B is wrong: The load remains.
D is wrong: Material properties remain.

questions.q: What does the principle of virtual work state?
options: Energy is created by the loads
For any admissible virtual displacement, internal virtual work equals external virtual work
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.4: Professor Bathe's course builds the finite element method on this principle.
A is wrong: It concerns virtual displacements.
B is wrong: That is not a work statement.
C is wrong: It is a balance of virtual work.

questions.q: What is the general formula for an element stiffness matrix?
options: The integral over the element of Bᵀ D B
The sum of the nodal forces
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.7: B relates nodal displacements to strains; D relates strains to stresses.
B is wrong: That is the element load vector.
C is wrong: That is only part of a bar's stiffness.
D is wrong: Stiffness relates forces to displacements.

questions.q: What are the consistent nodal loads for a two-node bar under a uniform load q over length L?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.8: They come from integrating the shape functions times the load.
A is wrong: That doubles the total.
B is wrong: The load is shared.
C is wrong: The units are wrong.

questions.q: What unknowns does an Euler-Bernoulli beam element have at each node?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.9: Four unknowns in all, with cubic shape functions.
A is wrong: Slopes must also be continuous.
B is wrong: Unknowns are displacements.
C is wrong: Those belong to other problems.

questions.q: What tip deflection does one Euler-Bernoulli beam element give for a cantilever with tip load P?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.10: A useful first test of any beam model.
A is wrong: That is the tip slope.
C is wrong: That is axial stretch.
D is wrong: That is a simply supported beam with a central load.

questions.q: When is a region commonly treated as thin enough for shell elements?
options: When its thickness is less than about a tenth of its other dimensions
When it is thicker than it is long
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.12: Shells carry membrane and bending action efficiently.
B is wrong: That is a solid.
C is wrong: Material does not decide.
D is wrong: Shells model structures.

questions.q: In steady heat conduction, what replaces displacement?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.15: Conductivity replaces stiffness and heat input replaces load.
A is wrong: That is for fluids.
C is wrong: Stress is not the unknown.
D is wrong: Steady problems have no time.

questions.q: What value does a node's shape function take at that node and at the other nodes?
options: One at its own node and zero at every other node
Zero at its own node and one elsewhere
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.2: Displacement is then the sum of nodal values times shape functions.
B is wrong: That is reversed.
C is wrong: Shape functions vary.
D is wrong: It multiplies the nodal displacement.

questions.q: Why must shape functions sum to one everywhere?
options: So that the stiffness matrix is diagonal
So that Gauss quadrature is exact
So that a rigid-body motion produces no strain
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.4: This is one of the three convergence requirements.
A is wrong: It is not diagonal.
B is wrong: That is a separate matter.
D is wrong: Unrelated to loads.

questions.q: What does the patch test check?
options: Whether a patch of elements reproduces a constant strain state exactly
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.5: Introduced by Bruce Irons.
A is wrong: It tests accuracy.
C is wrong: Not speed.
D is wrong: That is a reaction check.

questions.q: What does a negative Jacobian determinant in an element indicate?
options: The mapping from the parent element folds over, so the element is invalid
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.7: It often comes from a node dragged across its neighbours.
A is wrong: A perfect element has a positive Jacobian.
B is wrong: That causes volumetric locking.
D is wrong: Loads do not affect the Jacobian.

questions.q: With n Gauss points along a line, polynomials up to what degree are integrated exactly?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.9: A four-node quadrilateral normally uses two by two points.
A is wrong: Gauss quadrature does better than that.
B is wrong: Too low.
D is wrong: One degree too high.

questions.q: Which element is generally preferred to the four-node tetrahedron for stress analysis?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.11: Linear tetrahedra are too stiff in bending.
A is wrong: That is a 2D constant-strain element.
B is wrong: No such element is useful.
C is wrong: Not for solids.

questions.q: What causes volumetric locking?
options: A nearly incompressible material, with Poisson's ratio approaching one half
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.13: Mixed or hybrid formulations avoid it.
A is wrong: Locking is a formulation problem.
B is wrong: Not the cause.
D is wrong: Those cause singularities.

questions.q: What problem does reduced integration introduce?
options: Hourglass modes that produce no strain at the integration point
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.14: Codes add hourglass control, whose energy should be small.
A is wrong: Reduced integration is a remedy for locking.
B is wrong: That comes from distortion.
C is wrong: Those come from the geometry.

questions.q: What does mesh refinement reduce?
options: Discretisation error, but not modelling error
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.2: Wrong loads, supports, or materials are untouched by refinement.
A is wrong: Refinement cannot fix the model's equations.
C is wrong: Only discretisation error.
D is wrong: It reduces discretisation error.

questions.q: For elements of polynomial order p, how do stresses typically converge?
options: Not at all for any problem
In proportion to h to the power p, one order slower than displacements
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.4: Stresses come from derivatives of displacement.
A is wrong: They are slower.
B is wrong: Well-behaved problems converge.
C is wrong: Rarely so.

questions.q: How do compatible displacement-based models behave?
options: They are exact on any mesh
They are too stiff, so strain energy converges from below and deflections tend to be underestimated
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.6: A deflection larger than a careful hand calculation is a warning sign.
A is wrong: The opposite is true.
B is wrong: Not in general.
C is wrong: They tend to underestimate it.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of meshes recommended for a convergence study?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.7: Refined by a roughly constant factor, often two.
B is wrong: One mesh shows nothing about convergence.
C is wrong: Three are needed to see the trend and support extrapolation.
D is wrong: Three is the minimum, not ten.

questions.q: What does Richardson extrapolation use?
options: Results from several meshes to estimate the observed rate and the converged value
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.9: Roache's grid convergence index builds on it.
A is wrong: It needs several.
B is wrong: That is validation.
D is wrong: It uses mesh results.

questions.q: What happens to the peak stress at a sharp re-entrant corner as the mesh is refined?
options: It converges to three times the remote stress
It keeps rising, because linear elasticity predicts an infinite stress there
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.10: Such singularities are artefacts of the idealisation.
A is wrong: That is a circular hole.
C is wrong: It rises.
D is wrong: It never converges.

questions.q: What peak stress factor does a circular hole in a wide plate under tension have?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.13: A fine enough mesh reproduces this factor.
A is wrong: That is a sharp corner.
B is wrong: There is a concentration.
D is wrong: Too high.

questions.q: What is submodelling?
options: Solving a finely meshed local region with boundary displacements from a coarse global model
Meshing the global model finely everywhere
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.15: It relies on Saint-Venant's principle.
B is wrong: Not deletion.
C is wrong: Not the definition.
D is wrong: That is avoided.

questions.q: Why can a fully fixed support give misleading results?
options: It is infinitely stiff, unlike any real support
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.3: It stiffens the model and creates artificial edge stresses.
A is wrong: That is underconstraint.
B is wrong: Loads are unaffected.
D is wrong: The mesh is unaffected.

questions.q: A beam fixed at both ends is heated. Why might the model show large stresses?
options: The supports prevent thermal expansion, an overconstraint
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.4: Real structures often have sliding supports.
A is wrong: Not the reason given.
C is wrong: Mesh size is not the cause.
D is wrong: It causes expansion.

questions.q: Why should a force not be applied at a single node of a solid mesh?
options: It is a point load that produces a singular stress growing with refinement
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.6: Apply real forces as pressures over the true contact area.
A is wrong: They can.
B is wrong: Supports, not loads, control that.
C is wrong: The force is unchanged.

questions.q: Why can a half model with symmetry conditions be wrong for buckling or vibration?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.9: Use the full model, or run symmetric and antisymmetric conditions.
A is wrong: It does not.
B is wrong: Buckling has mode shapes.
D is wrong: It is allowed for static problems with symmetric loads.

questions.q: In the millimetre, newton, megapascal, tonne system, what is the density of steel?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.10: Mixing kilograms into this system gives masses a thousand times too large.
A is wrong: That is kilograms per cubic metre.
B is wrong: That is grams per cubic centimetre.
D is wrong: That is kilograms per cubic millimetre.

questions.q: Which is NOT an assumption of linear static analysis?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.12: Changing contact makes the problem nonlinear.
A is wrong: That is an assumption.
C is wrong: That is an assumption.
D is wrong: That is an assumption.

questions.q: Which eigenvalue problem gives natural frequencies and mode shapes?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.14: Modal analysis precedes dynamic response.
B is wrong: That is static equilibrium.
C is wrong: Stiffness is missing.
D is wrong: That is the stiffness integrand.

questions.q: What limits the time step of an explicit method such as central differences?
options: The time a stress wave takes to cross the smallest element
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.15: Explicit methods are only conditionally stable.
A is wrong: They are conditionally stable.
B is wrong: Not the limit.
D is wrong: Not a numerical limit.

questions.q: What is the difference between verification and validation?
options: Verification checks the equations are solved correctly; validation checks the right equations are solved
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.2: Verification is about mathematics, validation about physics.
B is wrong: They answer different questions.
C is wrong: It compares predictions with tests.
D is wrong: That is validation.

questions.q: Whose job is solution verification, such as a mesh convergence study?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.3: Code verification is mainly the developer's.
B is wrong: The vendor verifies the code.
C is wrong: That is validation.
D is wrong: It is required.

questions.q: What does NASA-STD-7009 ask analysts to document?
options: The credibility of a simulation, including verification, validation, input pedigree, and uncertainty
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.7: ASME V&V 10 covers verification and validation in computational solid mechanics.
A is wrong: It covers far more.
C is wrong: Not part of the standard.
D is wrong: It is about credibility.

questions.q: What is the first pitfall named in the course?
options: Believing the colour plot, whose highlighted maximum may be a singularity
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.8: Ask where the peak is, why, and whether it converges.
A is wrong: Not named first.
B is wrong: Hand calculations are recommended.
C is wrong: Documentation is recommended.

questions.q: For which material behaviour is von Mises stress the usual measure?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.10: Brittle materials and fatigue usually call for principal stresses or stress ranges.
A is wrong: Principal stresses suit brittle materials.
C is wrong: Fatigue uses stress ranges with a design code.
D is wrong: Not the measure discussed.

questions.q: What is the first step of the practical workflow?
options: Define the question, the quantities of interest, and the accuracy needed
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.11: Second is a hand estimate; third is geometry preparation.
B is wrong: That comes later.
C is wrong: That comes much later.
D is wrong: That comes last.
